# Significant results table
![](images/table.png){style="width:200px; background:white; border-radius:5px" fig-align="center"}

There are various output files in our output directory `genus_output`.
The first we will look at is the text file `significant_results.tsv`.
This contains all the significant features `maaslin3()` found.

This significance is based on the individual q-value or the joint q-value.
Additionally, the rows are ordered from most to least significant (i.e. ascending order based on the `qval_individual` column).

## Notebook setup
![](images/jupiter.png){style="width:150px; background:white; border-radius:5px; border: white solid 5px" fig-align="center"}

Save then close and halt your "2-MaAsLin3.ipynb" notebook.

Create and open a new jupyter notebook called "3-Text_output.ipynb".

Create a markdown cell at the top with:

```{r, eval=FALSE}
# 3-Text output
## Libraries
```

In a code cell load the required libraries.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
#Library
library("DT")
library("tidyverse")
```

## Read in and glimpsing
![](images/read.png){style="width:150px; background:white; border-radius:5px; border: white 5px solid" fig-align="center"}

To view the significant results we need to first read in the file.
In this case we'll read it in as a __tibble__ with [`readr::read_delim()`](https://neof-workshops.github.io/Tidyverse/readr/read.html) and then [glimpse](https://neof-workshops.github.io/Tidyverse/dplyr/glimpse.html) it.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
sig_res_tbl <- readr::read_delim(
    file="./genus_output/significant_results.tsv",
    delim="\t")
sig_res_tbl |> dplyr::glimpse()
```

There are many columns/variables which are explained in the next page: [Metrics](/maaslin3/metrics.qmd).

## Saving
![](images/save.png){style="width:150px; background:white; border-radius:5px; border: white 5px solid" fig-align="center"}

To load the significant results easily in other notebooks we'll save the `sig_res_tbl` object as a file.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
#Save significant reults tibble
save(sig_res_tbl, file="./genus_output/significant_results.RData")
```

## Viewing
![](images/eye_ibm_orange.png){style="width:150px; background:white; border-radius:5px; border: white 5px solid" fig-align="center"}

You can view the whole table in R:

```{r, eval=FALSE}
sig_res_tbl
```

With this object you can carry out various commands to pull out specific data.

Optionally, you can open the file (`significant_results.tsv`) by navigating to the `genus_output` directory through your jupyter file explorer.
Once in the directory you can click on the file to open it.

Neither of these methods are convenient.
In your own future analysis you can use excel but we'll show you another option below.

## HTML table creation
![](images/html.png){style="width:150px; background:white; border-radius:5px; border: white 5px solid" fig-align="center"}

We can create a html table with the package `DT` and its function `DT::datatable()`.
In the function we specify the `data.frame`/`tibble` to convert to HTML.
Additionally, we specify `options = list(pageLength = 20)` so the resulting html will show 20 rows at a time.

[`DT` package homepage](https://rstudio.github.io/DT/)

```{r, eval=FALSE}
#Convert table to html
sig_res_dt <- DT::datatable(sig_res_tbl, options = list(pageLength = 20))
```

The above code created an R object which we then need to save as an HTML file.
We'll carry this out with [`htmlwidgets::saveWidget()`](https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/htmlwidgets/versions/1.6.4/topics/saveWidget).
The option `selfcontained =` must be set to `TRUE` for this to function correctly.

[`htmlwidgets::savewdigets()` code documentation](https://www.htmlwidgets.org/develop_intro.html)

```{r, eval=FALSE}
#Save HTML
htmlwidgets::saveWidget(
    #Input widget/html
    widget = sig_res_dt,
    #Output html
    file = "./genus_output/significant_results.html",
    #Save as a single self contained HTML
    selfcontained = TRUE)
```

## Explore HTML table
![](images/html_explore.png){style="width:150px; background:white; border-radius:5px; border: white 5px solid" fig-align="center"}

With the HTML created navigate into the `genus_output` directory via the `jupyter` file browser.
Click on your HTML file (`significant_results.html`) to open it.

The html is interactive with the following features:

- Order the table by a specific column by clicking on its column name
    - Click on it once for descending order
    - Click on it twice for ascending order
- Set the number of rows to display with the drop down on the top left ("Show X entries")
    - Choices are: 10, 20, 25, 50, and 100
- Search for specific text/numbers with the search bar on the top right
    - Useful if you are interested in the results of a specific species or genus
- Navigate across the pages with the arrows and page numbers on the bottom right
- View the total number of rows (i.e. significant features) on the bottom left
